title: Cervical screening is still out of reach for millions. A test is only the beginning.
subtitle: WHO’s renewed call highlights a vast gap among women aged 30–49. Expanding access means making follow-up care as reachable as the screening itself.

paragraphs.text: The World Health Organization urged governments on 17 November to reach women who have never had cervical screening and ensure positive results lead to timely care, highlighting estimates that roughly three in five women aged 30–49 had never been screened.

The warning concerns a preventable cancer, but also a failure of access. A screening programme has to do more than offer a test: it must return results, arrange further assessment when needed and make treatment reachable.
WHO’s figures describe 2022, not a survey conducted this week. Their publication this year provides a benchmark against which governments’ newer promises can be judged.
What the numbers show

The analysis in The Lancet Global Health combined programme and population-based data to estimate coverage across 194 WHO member states and eight associated countries and territories. Researchers selected sources representative of screening in 2022 and checked preliminary estimates through country consultations.

An estimated 38% of women aged 30–49 had ever been screened, with a 95% confidence interval of 33–43%. For HPV testing specifically, coverage over the preceding five years was estimated at 2% in low- and middle-income countries, against 32% in high-income countries.

These are reconstructed population estimates, not one worldwide sample of women examined at the same time. They cannot establish how much access has changed since 2022 or show that a particular recent policy has already reduced cancer deaths.

WHO’s screening indicator draws on surveys and administrative estimates. Differences in the underlying information matter when interpreting comparisons. The broad disparity is clear; a precise account of today’s services requires newer local evidence.
Vaccination and screening serve different purposes

Persistent infection with cancer-causing types of human papillomavirus, or HPV, can produce cervical cell changes that eventually become cancer. Most HPV infections clear naturally. A positive HPV test is therefore not a cancer diagnosis.

Vaccination helps prevent infection, while screening identifies women who may need further assessment or treatment of precancerous changes. WHO’s global strategy links the two: by 2030, it seeks vaccination of 90% of girls by age 15, screening of 70% of women with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45, and appropriate treatment for 90% of women with precancer or invasive cancer.

Women who missed vaccination must not miss screening too, WHO’s noncommunicable-disease director Søren Brostrøm said in the agency’s announcement. His emphasis was on services reaching excluded women and on what happens after a positive result.

Self-sampling can give women another way to participate. WHO says it can expand access where HPV testing is part of a national programme, including for women who feel more comfortable collecting their own sample. It still requires a functioning service to process the sample and act on the result.
A national announcement is not universal access

Brazil illustrates the distinction. Its health ministry reported on 28 October that HPV DNA testing had reached the public health system in 26 of the country’s 27 federal units. But the detailed announcement specified that testing had begun in at least one municipality in each participating unit. That is a milestone in a gradual rollout, not proof that every eligible woman can obtain the test locally.

The ministry said conventional Pap testing remained available during the transition. Training covered both the new testing protocol and the organisation of follow-up care. Collection kits are produced by IBMP/Fiocruz; the ministry said it was also assessing other technologies meeting public-system quality standards. Equipment and procurement are only part of the service women need.

New Zealand is addressing a different barrier: the bill. Its government announced on 1 September that cervical screening would become free for all eligible women aged 25–69 from 1 March 2027. At the time of the announcement, ministers said about 55% of eligible women had to pay, with appointments costing NZ$35 to more than NZ$100.

Existing free provision covers groups including Māori and Pacific women, Community Services Card holders and women never screened or overdue. The wider offer is still a future commitment, not a service already available to everyone.

The government’s elimination plan also sets waiting-time targets. By 2030, it wants 80% of women referred for colposcopy to be seen within 30 working days and 90% with high-grade precancerous changes treated within 40 working days. Those are measurable promises about care beyond the initial test.
What women should be able to ask

For a reader considering screening, the useful questions are practical: am I eligible under my local programme, which test is offered, what will it cost, when will I receive the result, and who arranges any follow-up? Self-sampling availability and screening intervals depend on the programme and personal medical history.

Those questions also belong in public scrutiny of national campaigns. Governments should report how many previously unreached women complete screening and how many with abnormal results receive the recommended next step. Counting purchased kits or participating regions cannot answer either question.

ATHENA’s view is that prevention must be judged from the woman’s end of the service. An invitation she cannot afford to accept, or a result without an accessible next appointment, leaves the promise incomplete. The measure of progress is a continuous path from an informed choice to appropriate care.
The Athena Perspective.
